usage: I'll take the hot one, please.
Customer to barista; standard polite when picking hot over iced
반말 to a friend behind the counter or a very casual setting; rarely said to staff
거로 and 걸로 are both fine; 걸로 (걸=거+ㄹ) is the everyday spoken form
Natural extension: name the drink instead of just 'the hot one'
examples: "따뜻한 거 드릴까요?" "네, 따뜻한 걸로 주세요."
"Shall I make it hot?" "Yes, hot please."
걸로 answers a 'which one' question — it means 'the ~ one'
라떼 따뜻한 걸로 주세요. 시럽은 빼고요.
A hot latte, please. No syrup.
Adding a tweak: 빼고요 = 'leave it out'; -고요 softens a tacked-on request
밖이 너무 추워서요, 따뜻한 걸로 주세요. 큰 사이즈로요.
It's freezing outside, so a hot one please. Make it large.
Real flow: reason + order + size, all chained politely with -요
nuance: This is the customer's answer when staff ask hot or iced (따뜻한 거 / 아이스), or when you order unprompted. The choice particle -(으)로 attaches to the item you pick and means 'I'll go with the ~ one'; 걸로 is just 거 + 로 contracted, so 따뜻한 걸로 = 'the hot one, please' — much more natural than a full sentence. Register is plain polite -요, which covers every café and store; 반말 (따뜻한 거 줘) is only for friends, never for staff you don't know. The closest alternative is 핫으로 주세요 ('hot' as a loanword), which younger baristas accept, but 따뜻한 걸로 is the safe native choice and the dividing line is formality, not meaning. The classic English-speaker mistake is translating 'hot' as 뜨거운 — 뜨거운 means scalding/dangerously hot (a 뜨거운 냄비), whereas a warm drink is 따뜻한; ask for 뜨거운 거 and it sounds like you want to burn your tongue.

Dropping 로 and saying 따뜻한 거 주세요 — understandable but the 걸로 form ('the ~ one') is what signals you're choosing between options.
Using English 'hot one please' word order as 하나 따뜻한 주세요 — Korean puts the descriptor before the noun: 따뜻한 거 / 따뜻한 걸로.

usage: Customer to barista; the universal way to ask for a cold drink
반말 among friends; not used toward staff
Native equivalent; slightly more formal/older-sounding than 아이스로
Extension: 'iced americano' is so common it's clipped to 아아 in slang
examples: "따뜻한 거요, 아이스요?" "아이스로 주세요."
"Hot or iced?" "Iced, please."
아이스 is a loanword used as-is; -로 marks your choice
여름엔 무조건 아이스로 주세요. 얼음 많이요.
In summer always make it iced. Lots of ice.
얼음 많이요 = 'lots of ice'; -요 turns a noun phrase into a polite request
저는 아이스로 주시고, 친구는 따뜻한 걸로 주세요.
Iced for me, and hot for my friend.
Two orders in one breath; 주시고 links the first request to the second
nuance: 아이스로 주세요 is how you order any cold drink in Korea — 아이스 is the English 'ice' borrowed as a fixed word, and Koreans say it far more than the native 차가운 거. The particle -로 marks the option you're selecting ('go with iced'). It pairs directly against 따뜻한 걸로, and the dividing line between 아이스로 and 차가운 걸로 is feel: 아이스로 is the everyday café default, while 차가운 걸로 sounds a touch formal or is used for bottled drinks in a store. Register is polite -요 for all staff; 반말 only with friends. The English-speaker trap is asking for 얼음 주세요 ('give me ice') thinking it means 'iced' — that literally requests a cup of ice cubes; the temperature choice is 아이스로, and 얼음 is only the ice itself (useful in 얼음 많이요 / 얼음 빼고요).

Pronouncing it 'ice' English-style and stopping — Korean needs the particle: 아이스로 (with -로) to mark it as your selection.
Mixing it as 아이스 차가운 걸로 — redundant; pick one, 아이스로 or 차가운 걸로, not both.

usage: Staff to customer; the polite -ㄹ까요? offers to serve
반말 version; only a friend working the counter would say this
Which size would you like to go with?
A slightly more formal staff phrasing using 하시겠어요
As for size, which one shall I get you?
Extension with topic 는, common when listing options
examples: "사이즈 어떻게 드릴까요?" "작은 거로 주세요."
"What size?" "A small, please."
Answer with 작은/큰 거로; 드릴까요 is the staff side, 주세요 your side
"사이즈 어떻게 드릴까요?" "제일 큰 걸로요."
"What size?" "The biggest one."
제일 큰 = 'the biggest'; -요 alone can finish a short answer
"따뜻한 라떼요." "네, 사이즈 어떻게 드릴까요? 레귤러랑 라지 있어요."
"A hot latte." "Sure, what size? We have regular and large."
Staff often follow the size question by naming the options
nuance: This is a staff-to-customer line, so a learner mostly needs to recognize it and answer. 어떻게 드릴까요? literally 'how shall I give it to you?' is the polite service formula (드리다 is humble 'give', -ㄹ까요? offers/asks). You reply with a size + 거로/걸로: 작은 걸로요 / 큰 걸로요, or English sizes 톨/그란데/벤티 at chains. The near alternative the staff might use is 어떤 사이즈로 하시겠어요? — same meaning, a notch more formal. Politeness: staff always use 존댓말 to customers; you answer in plain polite -요. The English-speaker error is hearing 드릴까요 and freezing — don't translate it word-for-word; just catch 사이즈 and reply with the size. Another trap is answering 'medium' literally as 미디엄, which many Korean cafés don't use; they go 작은/큰 or 톨/그란데, so listen for the options they offer.

Saying 미디엄 expecting a medium — many cafés only have 작은/큰 or 톨/그란데/벤티; pick from what they list.

usage: Customer asking staff to log loyalty/stamp points to their account
반말; only with a friend, never with cashier staff
Softer, very polite variant using 부탁드리다
Can I earn points here too?
Extension: asking first whether the store has a points program
examples: "적립해 드릴까요?" "네, 적립해 주세요."
"Shall I add your points?" "Yes, please."
Staff offer with 드릴까요; you confirm with 주세요
적립해 주세요. 전화번호로요.
Add my points, please. By phone number.
전화번호로요 = 'by phone number', the usual way points are tracked
계산하기 전에 적립 먼저 해 주세요. 010-1234-5678이요.
Before you ring it up, add my points first. It's 010-1234-5678.
Real flow: ask to accrue, then read out your number
nuance: 적립 (積立) means 'accumulating/saving up', and 적립해 주세요 asks the cashier to credit loyalty points or stamps to you — by phone number, an app barcode, or a membership card. It's customer-to-staff, plain polite -요; 반말 (적립해 줘) is for friends only. The nearest alternatives are 적립 부탁드려요 (more deferential) and just showing your barcode while saying 적립이요 (most casual but fine). The dividing line is purely politeness, not meaning. A frequent English-speaker mistake is using 포인트 모아 주세요 thinking 'collect points' — Koreans don't phrase it that way; the verb is 적립하다. Also note this differs from 사용 (using) points: to spend them you say 적립금으로 결제할게요 or 포인트 쓸게요, so don't mix earning (적립) with redeeming.

mistakes: Saying 포인트 모아 주세요 ('gather points') — not the natural verb; use 적립하다: 적립해 주세요.
Confusing earning with spending — 적립 is earning; to redeem say 포인트로 결제할게요 / 포인트 쓸게요.
Forgetting to give the identifier — staff need your 전화번호, app barcode, or card; have it ready when you say 적립해 주세요.

usage: Shall I give you a bag?
Cashier to customer; -ㄹ까요? is the polite offer
반말; friend-to-friend phrasing, not store staff
Equally common staff version using 필요하세요
Shall I give you a bag separately?
Extension: 따로 = 'separately', since bags are usually charged
examples: "봉투 드릴까요?" "네, 주세요."
"Would you like a bag?" "Yes, please."
Answer 네 주세요 to accept, 아니요 괜찮아요 to decline
"봉투 드릴까요?" "아니요, 그냥 주세요."
"Need a bag?" "No, I'll just carry it."
그냥 주세요 = 'just hand it over (as is)', declining the bag
"봉투 드릴까요? 50원이에요." "네, 하나 주세요."
"Want a bag? It's 50 won." "Yes, one please."
Korean stores charge for bags; staff often state the price
nuance: Since Korea restricts free plastic bags, the cashier almost always asks 봉투 드릴까요? (드리다 humble 'give' + offer -ㄹ까요?) or 봉투 필요하세요?, and bags usually cost a small fee. This is staff-to-customer 존댓말; you just answer. To accept: 네, 주세요 or 하나 주세요; to decline: 아니요, 괜찮아요 / 그냥 주세요. The near-synonym 봉지 also means bag and is interchangeable in speech (봉지 드릴까요?), the line being only slight regional/personal preference. The English-speaker trap is answering 'okay' with 괜찮아요 meaning 'yes' — in Korean 괜찮아요 here means 'no thanks, I'm fine', so you'd end up refusing the bag you wanted; say 네, 주세요 to accept.

mistakes: Answering 괜찮아요 to mean 'yes/sure' — here it declines the bag; to accept say 네, 주세요.
Thinking bags are free and looking confused at the fee — Korean stores charge for 봉투; expect a small added cost.
Believing 봉투 and 봉지 are different items — both mean 'bag' here and are interchangeable; either answer works.

usage: Customer requesting a bag at checkout; plain polite
Could you give me a bag?
Extension: specify size with 큰/작은 걸로
examples: 봉투 주세요.
A bag, please.
The bare request when staff didn't offer one
봉투 하나 주세요. 음료수가 많아서요.
One bag, please. I've got a lot of drinks.
-아서요 gives a soft reason for needing it
이거 다 못 들겠어요. 봉투 두 개만 주세요.
I can't carry all this. Just two bags, please.
두 개만 = 'just two'; -만 limits the count politely
nuance: 봉투 주세요 is the customer side: you ask for a bag the cashier didn't offer (or accept the offer by stating it). Plain polite -요 covers all stores; 반말 봉투 줘 is friends-only. Soften it with 봉투 주시겠어요? or add a count (봉투 하나 주세요). Remember bags are usually paid, so saying 봉투 주세요 means you accept the small charge. The nearest alternative is 봉지 주세요 — fully interchangeable. The classic English-speaker error is requesting 가방 — 가방 is a backpack/handbag you wear, not a shopping bag; the disposable carry bag is 봉투/봉지. Another slip is over-using 주세요 abruptly without 네 when responding to an offer; if staff already asked 봉투 드릴까요?, answer 네, 주세요 rather than a flat 봉투 주세요.

Forgetting the bag is paid — 봉투 주세요 accepts the fee; don't be surprised by the small charge.
Replying to an offer with a bare 봉투 주세요 — when staff asked 봉투 드릴까요?, the natural accept is 네, 주세요.

english: Shall I heat it up for you?
usage: Convenience-store/café staff offering to microwave your food
반말; a friend offering, not staff
Shorter spoken staff variant of the same offer
Extension naming the item (도시락 / 삼각김밥 etc.)
examples: "데워 드릴까요?" "네, 데워 주세요."
"Shall I heat it up?" "Yes, please."
Staff offer with 드릴까요; you accept with 데워 주세요
"데워 드릴까요?" "아니요, 그냥 주세요."
"Want it heated?" "No, as it is, thanks."
그냥 주세요 declines heating and takes it cold
이 도시락 데워 주세요. 한 2분 정도요.
Please heat this lunchbox. About two minutes or so.
한 ~ 정도요 = 'about ~'; you can suggest the time
nuance: At 편의점 (convenience stores) and some cafés, staff offer 데워 드릴까요? for microwavable food — 도시락 lunchboxes, 삼각김밥 rice triangles, 컵라면-side items. 데우다 is 'to warm/heat up' (food specifically), so this is the right verb, not 끓이다 (boil) or 굽다 (grill). It's staff 존댓말; you accept with 데워 주세요 or decline with 그냥 주세요 / 괜찮아요. The near alternative is 따뜻하게 해 드릴까요? ('shall I make it warm?'), used loosely the same way; the dividing line is that 데우다 specifically means reheating in a microwave/heater. The English-speaker mistake is saying 뜨겁게 해 주세요 ('make it scalding') or using 요리해 주세요 ('cook it') — you only want it reheated, so the verb is 데우다: 데워 주세요.

Saying 끓여 주세요 ('boil it') for a lunchbox — 끓이다 is for liquids; microwaving solid food is 데우다.

usage: Café staff to customer; 드시고 가다 = eat here, 가져가다 = take out
반말; only between friends, not staff
More formal/standard register; 포장 = packed to go
Extension asking just the dine-in half
examples: "드시고 가세요, 가져가세요?" "가져갈게요."
"For here or to go?" "To go."
Answer 먹고 갈게요 (stay) or 가져갈게요 / 포장이요 (to go)
"드시고 가세요?" "네, 여기서 먹고 갈게요."
"Eating in?" "Yes, I'll have it here."
여기서 먹고 갈게요 clearly chooses dine-in
"드시고 가세요, 가져가세요?" "포장해 주세요. 따로 담아 주시고요."
"For here or to go?" "To go, please. And pack them separately."
포장해 주세요 = 'pack it to go'; the real takeout answer
nuance: This is the café's dine-in-or-takeout question. 드시다 is the honorific of 먹다, so 드시고 가세요? = 'will you eat (here) and go?'; 가져가세요? = 'will you take it away?'. It matters in Korea because dine-in drinks must use real cups/mugs by law while takeout uses disposables, and tax can differ. Staff use 존댓말; you answer with 먹고 갈게요 (stay) or 가져갈게요 / 포장이요 / 포장해 주세요 (to go). The more formal phrasing is 매장에서 드세요, 포장이세요?. The English-speaker error is replying 'to go' as 고 (the English word) or saying 테이크아웃 — 테이크아웃 is understood but the natural answers are 포장이요 or 가져갈게요. Another trap: using 먹다 about yourself is fine, but when staff ask they use the honorific 드시다 — don't 'correct' it to 먹고 가세요.

The more formal phrasing is 매장에서 드세요, 포장이세요?.

The English-speaker error is replying 'to go' as 고 (the English word) or saying 테이크아웃 — 테이크아웃 is understood but the natural answers are 포장이요 or 가져갈게요. Another trap: using 먹다 about yourself is fine, but when staff ask they use the honorific 드시다 — don't 'correct' it to 먹고 가세요.

Assuming dine-in and takeout are identical — dine-in uses real mugs (and may be taxed/priced differently), so the answer actually changes your cup.

usage: Customer asking for a to-go paper/plastic cup even while staying
Put it in a paper cup.
Please put it in a disposable cup.
Extension with 담다 ('to put/fill into'), a touch more polite
examples: "머그잔에 드릴까요?" "아니요, 일회용 컵에 주세요."
"In a mug?" "No, a disposable cup, please."
Used to override the default dine-in mug
여기서 마실 건데 일회용 컵에 주세요. 곧 나가야 해서요.
I'll drink here but in a disposable cup, please. I have to leave soon.
-ㄹ 건데 sets up a 'but'; gives a reason for the to-go cup
일회용 컵에 주시고, 캐리어도 하나 주세요.
A disposable cup, please, and a cup carrier too.
캐리어 = drink carrier; chained with 주시고

english: Please put it in my tumbler
usage: Customer handing over a personal cup; 담다 = put/fill into
Looser spoken variant; 해 주세요 stands in for 담아 주세요
I brought a tumbler — please fill this one.
Extension: announce the tumbler, then point and ask
examples: "텀블러에 담아 주세요." "네, 할인 들어가세요."
"In my tumbler, please." "Sure, you get a discount."
Bringing a tumbler usually earns a small discount in Korea
이 텀블러 깨끗해요. 여기에 담아 주세요.
This tumbler is clean. Please fill it here.
Reassuring it's clean; 여기에 = 'in here', 에 marks the destination
아이스 아메리카노 텀블러에 담아 주세요. 얼음 따로 주시고요.
An iced americano in my tumbler, please. And the ice separately.
Real flow: drink + tumbler + a side request, all chained

Bringing one usually earns a 텀블러 할인 (discount), so it's worth knowing. Customer-to-staff plain polite -요; 반말 with friends only. The destination particle is -에 (텀블러에), marking where the drink goes — not -로. The nearest alternative is the looser 텀블러에 해 주세요. The English-speaker mistake is using -로 (텀블러로 주세요), which sounds like 'give me a tumbler (as the item)' rather than 'pour into my tumbler'; with a container you're filling, use -에. Another slip is 채워 주세요 ('fill it up') — fine for a refill, but for a fresh drink the natural verb is 담다.

usage: The standard polite price question to any staff
반말; to a friend or familiar person
Extension: point with 이거 ('this one') at the item
examples: "얼마예요?" "4,500원입니다."
"How much?" "It's 4,500 won."
Staff answer with 원입니다; the bare question works anywhere
이 빵 얼마예요? 가격표가 없네요.
How much is this bread? There's no price tag.
-네요 notes a fresh observation (the missing tag)
다 해서 얼마예요? 카드 돼요?
How much all together? Do you take card?
다 해서 = 'all together'; a natural checkout combo

The dividing line with 얼마인가요? is just register/indirectness, not meaning. The English-speaker trap is writing 얼마에요 — the copula after a vowel-final 얼마 is 예요, not 에요 (얼마예요 is correct). Another slip is 얼마 있어요? which means 'how much (money) do you have?', not 'how much does it cost'; the price question is 얼마예요?. Korean prices are in 원 and spoken in 만/천 units, so listen for 사천오백 = 4,500.

usage: More formal -겠습니다, e.g. a business/formal setting
Extension with 계산하다 ('to pay/settle'), fully natural
examples: "현금이세요, 카드세요?" "카드로 할게요."
"Cash or card?" "By card."
-로 marks the means; -ㄹ게요 declares your intent
카드로 할게요. 일시불로요.
By card, please. In a single payment.
일시불 = 'lump-sum'; staff may ask 할부 (installments) vs 일시불
카드로 할게요. 여기 찍으면 돼요?
I'll use card. Do I tap it here?
찍다 here = 'tap/insert' the card; asking where the reader is

Another slip is the particle: it must be 카드'로' (by means of), not 카드를 or 카드에; -로 marks instrument.

english: Please give me a cash receipt
usage: Customer paying cash and asking for a tax-deductible receipt
A cash receipt to my phone number, please.
Extension: specify the number it should be registered to
examples: "현금영수증 해 드릴까요?" "네, 해 주세요."
"Shall I issue a cash receipt?" "Yes, please."
Staff offer with 해 드릴까요; you confirm with 해 주세요
현금으로 할게요. 현금영수증 해 주세요. 010-1234-5678이요.
I'll pay cash. And a cash receipt, please. It's 010-1234-5678.
Cash payment + receipt request + your number, in order
현금영수증 소득공제로 해 주세요.
Register the cash receipt for income deduction, please.
소득공제 (personal) vs 지출증빙 (business) — say which type

The English-speaker mistake is asking only for 영수증 and missing the tax benefit, or giving a card when you said cash — 현금영수증 only applies to 현금 (cash) payment.

usage: Customer asking staff where self-serve straws are
Extension: just ask staff for one directly
examples: "빨대 어디 있어요?" "저쪽 셀프바에 있어요."
"Where are the straws?" "Over at the self-serve bar."
셀프바 = self-serve station; 저쪽 = 'over there'
빨대 어디 있어요? 안 보여서요.
Where are the straws? I can't find them.
안 보여서요 = 'I don't see them', a soft reason for asking
빨대랑 휴지 어디 있어요?
Where are the straws and napkins?
랑 links two items; napkins (휴지/냅킨) are usually at the same bar
nuance: Most Korean cafés have a 셀프바 (self-serve bar) for straws, lids, napkins, sugar, and water, so 빨대 어디 있어요? ('where are the straws?') is the practical question. 빨대 literally 'sucking stick' = straw. 어디 있어요? = 'where is it?'. Plain polite -요; 반말 with friends. If you'd rather have staff fetch one, say 빨대 좀 주세요 instead — the line is whether you locate it yourself (어디 있어요?) or have them hand it over (주세요). The English-speaker mistake is the location verb: it's 어디 있어요? (existence/location), not 어디예요? — 어디예요? asks 'where is (this place)?' and sounds odd about objects. Expecting staff to bring it unasked — straws are usually self-serve at the 셀프바; either find it or say 빨대 좀 주세요.

usage: Customer asking staff if there's a free table/seat
Are there seats, by any chance?
Is there a table for two?
Extension: state the party size with 명
examples: "자리 있어요?" "네, 2층에 있어요."
"Any seats?" "Yes, upstairs on the 2nd floor."
Staff often direct you (2층 = 2nd floor) rather than seat you
혹시 자리 있어요? 콘센트 있는 자리면 좋겠어요.
Any seats, by chance? A spot with an outlet would be great.
혹시 softens the ask; 콘센트 자리 = a seat with a power outlet
지금 자리 있어요? 두 명인데요.
Any seats right now? There are two of us.
-인데요 tacks on context (party size) and invites a reply

english: To go, please / Pack it up

Extension: ask first whether takeout is possible
examples: "드시고 가세요?" "아니요, 포장해 주세요."
"Eating in?" "No, to go, please."
The natural takeout answer to the dine-in question
라떼 한 잔 포장해 주세요. 캐리어도 주시고요.
One latte to go, please. With a carrier too.
캐리어 = drink carrier; 주시고요 adds the second request
남은 거 포장해 주세요. 집에서 먹을게요.

Another option is 싸 주세요 ('wrap it up'), fine and homey for leftovers but slightly informal for a café order; 포장해 주세요 is the clean default.
포장 (包裝) literally means 'wrapping/packaging'.
The English-speaker mistake is 테이크아웃 해 주세요 — understood, but 포장 is the natural native word, and 테이크아웃 컵 is more for the cup itself.

mistakes: Defaulting to 테이크아웃 해 주세요 — understood but the natural word is 포장: 포장해 주세요.
Confusing it with dine-in answers — 포장해 주세요 is takeout; to stay say 먹고 갈게요 / 여기서 먹을게요.
Using 포장 for gift-wrapping expectations — in a café it means 'pack to go'; for gift wrap you'd specify 선물 포장.
